newsitem.title: UK: UK says African force should take over in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UK says African force should take over in Zaire.

text.p: Britain said on Thursday the proposed multinational force to be sent to help a million starving refugees in Zaire should aim to hand over control quickly to African forces.
Defence Minister Michael Portillo said it was crucial that the Canadian-led force should not allow itself to be drawn into the conflict between Tutsi rebels and their Hutu foes.
"I see Western forces as really being the only ones who can go into a dangerous situation and stabilise it," he told BBC radio in a live interview.

"I also believe it should be our objective to hand over the operations, quite quickly within a very few months, to African forces -- I include South African forces in that -- who would then be able to continue with the situation that we had stabilised," he said.

Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind said the nations contributing to the humanitarian force planned to pull their troops out after three or four months but said many details of the proposed mission had to be decided.
"Let me be frank -- I don't think that at this moment in time we can say it is yet as clearly defined as we would like," he told BBC radio in Paris.

"We accept that there is a need for a force go out there and that we should be part of that...but there is a lot more work to be done over the next few days to clarify the mandate, to ensure that it is limited to humanitarian aid."

As he spoke, heavy fighting between rebels and Hutus erupted around the eastern Zairean town of Goma, underlining the complexity of the task facing the force, which would try to open up aid routes to the refugees caught up in the confict.

Portillo was due to make a statement to parliament at 3.30 p.m. (1530 GMT) to outline Britain's contribution.Military sources said a rapid deployment force of up to 3,500 troops would start to move as early as next week.

"I believe we will make things better in the sense that we will get people fed but amongst the objectives we need to clarify is just what our attitude is going to be to the armed people who presently infest the refugee camps," Portillo said.
"I think it's extremely important that we should not now be drawn into taking sides or drawn into Central African politics."

The United Nations envoy negotiating a mandate for the force with Rwanda and Zaire, whose army is battling Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels, said it was unclear how the Canadian-led troops could handle armed Hutus using refugees as a screen.
Most are former soldiers of the Rwanda armed forces who fled with Hutu civilians after losing a civil war following the 1994 massacre of Tutsis in Rwanda.

"Provided we go sufficiently robustly armed then the warring factions, although they are dangerous, naturally do not want to take on much better-armed and equipped and commanded troops. So we shall certainly make sure our forces are properly equipped in order to defend themselves," said Portillo.
A meeting will take place in New York on Thursday bringing together all parties interested in aiding the refugees.
